summary: Learners aged 9-10 practise the engineering-design practice of generating AND comparing [curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS3-2] hazards (earthquakes, floods, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions) on humans. The load-bearing idea: you cannot stop the natural event, you can only reduce its IMPACT, and engineers choose by comparing several distinct options against explicit criteria (effectiveness, cost, feasibility) and weighing trade-offs — there is no single universally 'best' solution, only the best fit for the criteria that matter.
misconceptions: The goal is to STOP the disaster (we reduce its impact on people/property; we can't prevent the natural event).
There is one single correct solution (engineering compares multiple options against criteria; the best depends on priorities).
The best solution is simply the most effective one (cost and feasibility matter — trade-offs decide).
A warning system or a strong building alone solves everything (layered solutions — engineering + warnings + preparedness — work together).
More expensive always means better (not necessarily — effectiveness and feasibility must be weighed too).

activities.title: Hazard-solutions design bench: generate then compare
steps: Choose a hazard for a specific place (e.g. a flood-prone coastal town, an earthquake zone, a region near an active volcano).

Generate at least three DISTINCT solutions drawn from different families: engineering (sea wall, flood barriers, earthquake-resistant buildings, raised houses), warning systems (tsunami/eruption alerts, sirens), and preparedness/planning (evacuation routes, drills, land-use planning).
Enter each solution into a comparison grid with columns for effectiveness, cost and feasibility.
Weight the criteria differently (e.g. prioritise 'lowest cost' then prioritise 'most lives saved') and observe how the preferred choice changes.
Run or describe a hazard scenario for each option to estimate how much impact it might reduce, and confirm that none of them stops the hazard itself.
State a recommendation and justify it from the comparison and the criteria that matter most here.
activities.insight: Engineers generate multiple options and compare them on explicit criteria; the 'best' solution depends on which criteria are prioritised, trade-offs typically arise, and solutions reduce impact rather than eliminate the hazard.

activities.title: Consolidation: sort, rank and choose under criteria
steps: Sort a set of measures into solution families: engineering, warning systems, preparedness/planning.
Order several solutions by cost, then re-order them by effectiveness, and notice how the orderings differ.
Answer constrained-choice questions such as 'Given a tight budget, which solution best fits?' and justify the choice against the stated criterion.
activities.insight: Protective measures can be grouped into families (engineering, warning systems, preparedness/planning), and ranking the same options on different criteria can produce different 'winners', reinforcing that choice is criteria-dependent.

activities.title: Explore a resilient-community scene
steps: Examine an annotated town scene and reveal each protective feature in turn: earthquake-resistant buildings, flood barriers, warning sirens, evacuation routes.
For each revealed feature, read or state its pros and cons.
Answer the prompt 'Can we stop the earthquake/flood?' and check the response: no — we reduce its impact.
activities.insight: There is a menu of real solution families, and the overall goal is reducing harm to people and property, not preventing the natural event.

activities.title: Pressure-test ideas with an engineer persona (optional complement)
steps: Propose each solution to a disaster-planner or civil-engineer character.
Respond to challenges such as 'What will that cost?' and 'Is it feasible here?'
Revise or defend proposals in light of the questioning.
activities.insight: Articulating and defending proposals against criteria is intended to rehearse and strengthen the generative, reasoning side of design.

checkQuestion: Here's a town near the coast that faces earthquakes and the risk of flooding. Your job: come up with at least two or three different solutions to reduce the harm, then compare them and recommend which to use — explaining how you decided.
checkAnswer: The child names the hazards and their impacts, GENERATES several distinct solutions (e.g. earthquake-resistant buildings, sea wall/flood barriers, an early-warning system, evacuation routes), and COMPARES them against criteria like effectiveness, cost and feasibility — justifying a recommendation from that comparison and recognising no single solution fixes everything.
